subject: physics
title: Required practicals: electricity
key_idea: Three practicals test the electricity theory. Resistivity comes from the gradient of a graph of resistance against length. E.m.f. and internal resistance come from the intercept and gradient of a graph of terminal p.d. against current. A thermistor in a potential divider can be calibrated to act as a thermostat.

sections.heading: Determining the resistivity of a material

blocks.text: Measure the resistance of different lengths of a wire of known diameter, then use R = ρL / A.

items.text: Use a micrometer to measure the diameter at several points along the wire and in two perpendicular directions. Take the mean and find A = πd²/4.
Connect the wire in series with a cell and an ammeter. Connect a voltmeter across the wire.
Clip to the wire at measured lengths along a metre rule, for example every 10 cm from 10 cm to 100 cm.
At each length record V and I, and calculate R = V / I. Keep the current small and switch off between readings.
Plot R against L. Draw the line of best fit through the origin.
The gradient is ρ / A, so ρ = gradient × A.

items: A small current prevents the wire heating, which would raise its resistance.
The diameter is the biggest source of uncertainty, because A depends on d², so a small percentage error in d doubles in A.
Poor contact at the clip, or a zero error on the ammeter, gives a non-zero intercept.
Repeat the readings and average, and check the ammeter for zero errors.
ρ = gradient of R against L × cross-sectional area.
Use a low current, and measure d with a micrometer at several places.

sections.heading: Determining the e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell

blocks.text: Change the current taken from a cell and record its terminal p.d.

items.text: Connect the cell, an ammeter, a switch and a variable resistor in series. Connect a voltmeter across the cell terminals.
Close the switch, adjust the variable resistor and record V and I. Do at least six readings across a wide range of current.
Open the switch between readings, so the cell does not warm up or run down.
Plot V against I. Use V = E − Ir to find E from the y-intercept and r from the negative of the gradient.

items: A cell with a small internal resistance gives a shallow line, so use as wide a range of current as is safe.
A large current heats the cell and changes r, so switch off between readings.
Read the intercept from a graph that extends back to I = 0, not by extrapolating from a small range.
V = E − Ir: y-intercept = E, gradient = −r.
Switch off between readings to stop the cell warming.

sections.heading: Calibrating a thermistor as a thermostat

blocks.text: An NTC thermistor in a potential divider gives an output p.d. that changes with temperature. A calibration graph turns that p.d. into a temperature.

items.text: Connect the thermistor in series with a fixed resistor across a supply of known p.d. Connect a voltmeter across the fixed resistor.
Place the thermistor in a waterproof sleeve in a beaker of water, with a thermometer beside it.
Change the water temperature in steps, for example every 10 °C from near 0 °C to near 80 °C. Stir, wait for the temperature to settle, then record the temperature and the output p.d.
Plot output p.d. against temperature and draw a smooth curve. Use it to read the p.d. that matches the switching temperature.
Set a comparator or switching circuit to operate at that p.d., so the circuit switches a heater at the chosen temperature.

diagram.alt: Put the steps for calibrating a thermistor as a thermostat in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps of the calibration in order.
steps: Connect the thermistor and fixed resistor in series across the supply.
Place the thermistor in a water bath beside a thermometer.
Stir and let the water settle at each temperature.
Record the temperature and the output p.d.
Read off the p.d. for the switching temperature and set the switching circuit to it.

items: Stirring and waiting make the thermistor temperature equal the thermometer reading.
Using a thermistor in a sleeve keeps water away from the electrical contacts.
A small current avoids heating the thermistor above the water temperature.
The output p.d. across the fixed resistor rises as the temperature rises, because the thermistor resistance falls.
The output p.d. is calibrated against temperature using a water bath.
Stir and wait so the thermistor and thermometer agree.

checks.q: In the resistivity experiment, the gradient of a graph of R against L is 5.2 Ω/m and the wire's diameter is 0.28 mm. Calculate the resistivity.
A graph of terminal p.d. against current for a cell is a straight line from 1.55 V at 0 A to 1.10 V at 0.90 A. State the e.m.f. and calculate the internal resistance.
Explain why the water must be stirred and left to settle before each reading when calibrating the thermistor.
checks.a: Stirring makes the temperature the same throughout the water, and waiting lets the thermistor reach the same temperature as the thermometer, so the p.d. matches the recorded temperature.
